Financial System Report 
October 2025 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
The total of major banks, regional banks, and shinkin banks covered in this Report is as follows (as of 
end-September 2025). 
 
Major banks comprise the following 10 banks: Mizuho Bank, MUFG Bank, Sumitomo Mitsui Banking 
Corporation, Resona Bank, Saitama Resona Bank, Mitsubishi UFJ Trust and Banking Corporation, 
Mizuho Trust and Banking Company, Sumitomo Mitsui Trust Bank, SBI Shinsei Bank, and Aozora Bank. 
Regional banks comprise the 61 member banks of the Regional Banks Association of Japan (regional 
banks I) and the 36 member banks of the Second Association of Regional Banks (regional banks II). 
Shinkin banks are the 247 shinkin banks that hold current accounts at the Bank of Japan. 
 
This Report basically uses data available as of end-September 2025.

Objectives of the Financial System Report 
The Bank of Japan's Financial System Report has two main objectives. The first is to assess the 
stability of Japan's financial system. The second is to communicate with all related parties on the 
future tasks and challenges in order to ensure the system's stability. 
The Report assesses the vulnerabilities of the financial system from a macroprudential perspective. 
Within a macroprudential framework, institutional designs and policy measures are developed 
based on risk assessments in the financial system in order to ensure the stability of the overall 
financial system. In so doing, the interconnectedness of the real economy, financial markets, and 
financial institutions' behavior are taken into account. 
The Bank uses the results of the analysis set out in the Report in planning policies to ensure the 
stability of the financial system and for providing guidance and advice to financial institutions 
through on-site examinations and off-site monitoring. It makes use of the results in international 
discussions on regulation, supervision, and vulnerability assessment. In relation to the conduct of 
monetary policy, the macro assessment of financial system stability is also regarded as important 
input for the Bank in assessing risks in economic and price developments from a medium- to long-
term perspective. 
Motivations behind the October 2025 issue 
At the beginning of April 2025, asset prices fluctuated significantly in global financial markets due 
to heightened uncertainties regarding trade policies in each jurisdiction. Currently, uncertainties 
remain high regarding the formulation of economic policies in each jurisdiction, and regarding 
geopolitical risks and developments in global financial markets. This Report analyzes the following 
four points. 
First, this Report analyzes the effects of changes in trade and other policies in each jurisdiction on 
domestic corporate sector and banks' credit costs. As a result of changes in trade and other policies 
in each jurisdiction triggered by, for example, the materialization of geopolitical risks, global trade 
volume could fall substantially, adversely affecting corporate profits. This Report also provides an 
analysis of the resilience of the financial system if such tail risks were to materialize.  
Second, with regard to stock and real estate prices, the transaction environment in each market is 
examined, thereby providing an analysis of potential future risks. 
Third, this Report explores the possibility that foreign non-bank financial intermediaries (NBFIs), 
such as hedge funds, which have been increasing their presence both domestically and 
internationally, may have an effect on Japanese financial markets, particularly through the rapid 
unwinding of investment positions. 
Fourth, this Report provides updates on the effects of changes in the interest rate environment on 
banks, households, and firms. With regard to developments in deposits, this Report examines the 
effects of structural factors such as demographic changes and the spread of digital channels, and 
those of other factors that affect bank deposits amid rising interest rates.

I. Executive summary: Stability assessment of Japan's financial system

I. Executive summary: Stability assessment of Japan's financial system 
Japan's financial system has been maintaining stability on the whole. 
In the loan market, financial intermediation has continued to function smoothly as firms' demand 
for loans has continued to rise and banks' lending stance has remained active. Under such 
circumstances, no major financial imbalances have been seen in current financial activities. 
Japanese banks have sufficient capital bases and stable funding bases to withstand significant 
stresses, including those equivalent to the global financial crisis that would cause major corrections 
in financial markets and the real economy at home and abroad, as well as those with compound 
factors particularly resulting from the materialization of geopolitical risks that would cause a 
substantial decline in global trade volume, and lead to global increases in inflation and interest 
rates. However, uncertainties remain high regarding the formulation of economic policies in each 
jurisdiction, and regarding geopolitical risks, and developments in global financial markets. 
Financial institutions need to be vigilant against the materialization of various risks. From a long-
term perspective, if structural factors remain, such as a decline in firms' loan demand reflecting the 
shrinking population and other factors, banks' profitability and loss-absorbing capacity could decline, 
depending on the supply and demand balance in the loan market, and this could lead to a 
contraction of financial intermediation activities or an overheating, such as excessive search for 
yield. From the perspective of maintaining stability in Japan's financial system, close attention is 
warranted on future developments in the financial system, while examining both overheating and 
contraction risks (Chart I-1). 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Developments in asset prices  Chapters II, IV-B, and V-A 
In global financial markets, at the beginning of April, stock prices fell substantially as market 
sentiment became significantly cautious, reflecting the heightened uncertainties regarding trade 
policy in each jurisdiction. Since then, prices of risky assets have risen, with market sentiment 
improving, reflecting factors such as progress in trade negotiations. The heat map shows that stock 
prices has been "red," which signals an upward deviation from the trend (Chart I-1). In terms of 
stock valuations as of the end of September, price-earnings (P/E) ratios remain generally at 
historical average levels while risk premiums indicated by the equity yield spreads, i.e., the 
difference between expected equity yields and 10-year Japanese government bond (JGB) yields, 
have declined somewhat (left panel of Chart I-2). Given that uncertainties regarding the formulation 
of trade and other economic policies in each jurisdiction remain high, sentiment in global financial 
markets could become cautious. Given that Japanese banks have a certain amount of market risk 
associated with stockholdings, close attention should be paid to developments in risky asset prices, 
including stock prices.

Real estate prices have been rising, particularly in major metropolitan areas (Chart I-3). The rise in

Corporate bankruptcies and defaults and the effects of trade and other policies in each 
jurisdiction  Chapters IV-A and VI-B  
Amid the continuing moderate economic recovery, corporate profits in Japan have been improving 
on the whole, and the proportion of firms that are either making operating losses with negative net 
worth or are making operating losses, which increased during the pandemic, has been falling. 
Corporate bankruptcies and defaults have been more or less unchanged, albeit with fluctuations  
(Chart I-5). However, it is necessary to bear in mind that  labor shortages, rising labor costs and 
rises in raw material prices may be adding further pressure. 
Japan's corporate sector appears to be reasonably resilient to the effects of changes in trade and 
other policies in each jurisdiction. The profit projections released by large firms reveal that,  given 
that their financial positions leading up to the current stress are favorable,  large firms' debt 
repayment capacity seems to be maintained overall despite the effects of changes in trade and 
other policies in each jurisdiction (left panel of Chart I-6). As for small and medium-sized enterprises 
(SMEs), the effects on their profits and default rates are likely limited overall, as many SMEs have 
ample on-hand liquidity (middle and right panels of Chart I-6). However, if the stress caused by 
changes in trade and other policies turns out to have a larger impact on profits than assumed in 
the projections, debt repayment capacity could deteriorate significantly among firms whose 
financial positions are relatively vulnerable, including small and medium-sized supplier firms.  In 
exporting industries, the proportion of large loans tends to be high; therefore, attention is also 
warranted to the fact that if individual firms were downgraded, the impact on credit costs could be 
significant.

II. Risks observed in financial and capital markets 
 Looking at developments during the first half of fiscal 2025, stock prices fell substantially 
and credit spreads on corporate bonds widened in global financial markets at the beginning 
of April, as market sentiment became significantly cautious, reflecting heightened 
uncertainties regarding trade policy in each jurisdiction. Thereafter, however, prices of risky 
assets rose, with market sentiment improving, reflecting factors such as progress in trade 
negotiations.1 
 In Japanese financial markets, stock prices fell substantially at the beginning of April, mainly 
due to the effects of increasingly cautious market sentiment in global financial markets. 
Thereafter, they increased significantly reflecting the agreement in tariff negotiations 
between Japan and the United States, while following the recovery in U.S. stock prices. 
Long-term interest rates rose over the first half of fiscal 2025, albeit with fluctuations 
reflecting progress in trade negotiations and changes in market participants' views on the 
future conduct of monetary policy by the Bank of Japan. 
 Uncertainty about financial markets remains high. Specifically, attention has been drawn to 
uncertainties over how trade and other policies in each jurisdiction will evolve and how 
economic activity and prices at home and abroad will react to them. Market participants have 
also paid attention to geopolitical risks, developments in major foreign high-tech stocks, and 
the course of fiscal policy in each jurisdiction. In this situation, attention should continue to 
be paid to the possibility that global financial conditions could tighten through such factors 
as sharp repricing of risky assets and a deterioration in the dollar funding environment. 
A. Global financial markets during the first half of fiscal 2025 
Looking at developments during the first half of fiscal 2025, stock prices fell substantially and credit 
spreads on corporate bonds widened in global financial markets at the beginning of April, as market 
sentiment became significantly cautious, reflecting heightened uncertainties regarding trade policy 
in each jurisdiction. Thereafter, however, prices of risky assets rose, with market sentiment 
improving, reflecting factors such as progress in trade negotiations. 
U.S. and European bond markets 
U.S. long-term interest rates were more or less flat over the first half of fiscal 2025 (Chart II-1-1). 
They declined at the beginning of April amid a deterioration in market sentiment, reflecting 
heightened uncertainties regarding trade policy in each jurisdiction. Thereafter, although they 
temporarily rose with the improvement in market sentiment owing to progress in trade negotiations, 
they became more or less flat as expectations of policy interest rate cuts by the Federal Reserve 
heightened in response to weak U.S. economic indicators. The yield curve for U.S. Treasuries 
steepened in reflection of such factors as growing expectations of policy interest rate cuts by the 
Federal Reserve and concerns over a deterioration in supply and demand conditions in U.S. 
Treasuries due to expansionary fiscal policy. European long-term interest rates were more or less 
flat over the first half of fiscal 2025. They decreased at the beginning of April in tandem with U.S. 
interest rates. Thereafter, the German government decided to issue additional government bonds 
in line with the country's increased defense spending, and this led European long-term interest

U.S. and European credit markets 
In U.S. and European credit markets, credit spreads on both investment-grade bonds and high-
yield bonds narrowed over the first half of fiscal 2025; despite widening at the beginning of April, 
when market sentiment deteriorated, they subsequently began to narrow in line with the 
improvement in market sentiment (left panel of Chart II-1-3). Looking at the distribution of credit 
spreads on U.S. high-yield bonds, the overall level of spreads remained low, although spreads on 
some of these bonds remained wide due to the cumulative effects of the high interest rate 
environment (middle panel of Chart II-1-3). Meanwhile, the default rates of both high-yield bonds 
and leveraged loans, which had risen, mainly reflecting the cumulative effects of the high interest 
rate environment, remained more or less flat from the start of 2025 (right panel of Chart II-1-3). 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Emerging markets and international commodity markets 
In emerging markets, stock prices rose substantially over the first half of fiscal 2025, moving 
generally in tandem with U.S. stock prices. Currencies in emerging markets appreciated amid the 
trend in the dollar's depreciation, reflecting such factors as uncertainty surrounding the future policy 
conduct of the U.S. administration (Chart II-1-4). In this situation, looking at net flows of emerging 
market funds, both bond funds and equity funds saw net outflows in April when market sentiment 
became cautious; however, they subsequently experienced sustained net inflows, with fluctuations 
smoothed out. 
In international commodity markets, prices of crude oil declined at the beginning of April, due to 
concerns that trade policy in each jurisdiction could cause a global economic slowdown (Chart II-
1-5). Although prices of crude oil temporarily increased thereafter due mainly to concerns over 
geopolitical risks in the Middle East, they declined over the first half of fiscal 2025, driven by weak 
U.S. economic indicators and an increase in production by oil-producing economies.

With regard to term interest rates, the 3-month overnight index swap rate rose slightly over the first 
half of fiscal 2025, as expectations of a policy interest rate hike by the Bank grew (right panel of 
Chart II-2-1). Meanwhile, yields on 3-month T-bills increased slightly, albeit with fluctuations due to 
demand from domestic and foreign investors. 
Japanese government bond (JGB) markets 
Long-term interest rates increased over the first half of fiscal 2025; they declined significantly at the 
beginning of April, due mainly to declining expectations of a policy interest rate hike by the Bank, 
reflecting heightened uncertainties regarding trade policy in each jurisdiction; however, rates 
subsequently increased against the background of a rise in interest rates in the United States and 
Europe due to the improvement in market sentiment, as well as growing expectations of a policy 
interest rate hike by the Bank reflecting the agreement in tariff negotiations between Japan and the 
United States and other factors (Chart II-2-2). The yield curve for JGBs steepened, driven by a rise 
in super-long-term yields, as attention was paid to fiscal expansion globally. In the meantime, the 
implied volatility of JGB futures continued to be at a high level (Chart II-1-1). 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Liquidity and functioning of JGB markets 
The liquidity and functioning of JGB markets continued to improve, following a significant decline 
at the beginning of April. 2 Among liquidity indicators in JGB markets,  bid-ask spreads of newly 
issued bonds and market resiliency in the JGB futures market deteriorated at the beginning of April, 
reflecting a decline in market participants' risk tolerance. They subsequently began to recover in 
line with the improvement in market sentiment (Charts II-2-3 and II-2-4). According to the Bank's 
Bond Market Survey , the diffusion index for the degree of bond market functioning, despite 
remaining negative, also showed an improvement in the August survey, after a significant decline 
within negative territory in the May survey. This development is consistent with the trends in liquidity 
indicators (Chart II-2-5). The reduction of the Bank's purchase amount of JGBs from August 2024 
likely led to enhanced market functioning through an improvement in liquidity, mainly of newly 
issued bonds.

C. Risks to financial markets 
Uncertainty about financial markets remains high. Specifically, attention has been drawn to 
uncertainties over how trade and other policies in each jurisdiction will evolve and how economic 
activity and prices at home and abroad will react to them. Market participants have also paid 
attention to geopolitical risks, developments in major foreign high-tech stocks, and the course of 
fiscal policy in each jurisdiction. 
In stock markets, amid continued high uncertainties regarding trade policy in each jurisdiction, 
attention is warranted to the risks that market sentiment will deteriorate again due to concerns over 
a global economic slowdown, and that interest rates will remain elevated, driven by a reacceleration 
in inflation in the United States. In addition, there has also been vigilance against the risk of price 
adjustments for major foreign high-tech stocks that have recently experienced rapid price increases. 
In bond markets, market participants have focused their attention on the future conduct of monetary 
policy and developments in fiscal policy in each jurisdiction . In credit markets, as the cumulative 
effects of the high-interest rate environment remain in the United States and Europe, the risk of 
deterioration in financial conditions of firms with low credit ratings and those with high leverage 
ratios, particularly if economic activity decelerates, continues to draw attention. In the U.S. and 
European real estate industries, attention has continued to be paid to developments in commercial 
real estate, mainly reflecting elevated vacancy rates for office buildings. 
In emerging markets, there have been concerns over the risk that capital outflows from countries 
with fiscal and financial vulnerability could occur, with attention continuing to be paid to the 
possibility that trade policy in each jurisdiction will put downward pressure on the economy, mainly 
through global trade developments. In international commodity markets, geopolitical factors and 
uncertainty over developments in the Chinese economy, which have a significant impact on 
commodity and grain prices, warrant attention. 
Attention should continue to be paid to the possibility that the materialization of these risks could 
lead to tightening in global financial conditions through such factors as sharp repricing of risky 
assets and a deterioration in the dollar funding environment.

III. Financial intermediation 
 Financial intermediation has continued to function smoothly in Japan. Despite the increase 
in domestic lending rates, firms' demand for loans has continued to rise mainly on the back 
of economic recovery and developments in mergers and acquisition (M&A) deals. Banks' 
lending stance has also been active. As for foreign lending, major banks have been selective 
amid concerns over uncertainty regarding future developments in foreign economies. 
Meanwhile, banks have been cautious about making securities investment amid concerns 
over the risk of higher interest rates in Japan. 
 Assets under management held by non-bank financial intermediaries (NBFIs) in Japan have 
remained on an uptrend. Investment funds' assets under management have remained on 
an increasing trend on the back of inflows of funds from households. An increase in financial 
dealers and brokers' short-term repo transactions has continued on both the asset and 
liability sides. Life insurance companies' accumulation of holdings of super-long-term 
Japanese government bonds (JGBs) has reached a plateau as they have mostly finished 
making adjustments to comply with new regulations. 
A. Financial intermediation by the banking sector 
1. Loans 
The annual growth rate of domestic loans by privately-owned banks has been at around 3.5 percent 
(Chart III-1-1). In addition to an increase in loan demand reflecting M&A deals and demand for real 
estate-related loans, demand for working capital amid the recovery in economic activity has been 
rising. Downward pressure stemming from repayments on effectively interest-free and unsecured 
loans (so-called zero-zero loans) on the outstanding amount of loans by regional and shinkin banks 
has been abating. Loans to both large and medium-sized firms and small firms have continued to 
increase (Chart III-1-2).

 The quality of banks' domestic and foreign loan portfolios has been maintained. Even in a 
situation where uncertainties regarding trade and other policies in each jurisdiction have 
remained high, credit costs have been limited so far. With corporate profits in Japan having 
been on an improving trend on the whole, corporate bankruptcies have been more or less 
unchanged, despite some fluctuations. The quality of banks' foreign loan portfolios has 
continued to be maintained as banks have been selective in their foreign lending.

denominated bonds, and their securities portfolios show that overall interest rate risk has 
generally been unchanged for major banks, while it has been on a slight downtrend for

continue to adequately manage market risks.  
 Banks have sufficient yen funding liquidity, which mainly consists of small retail deposits. As 
for foreign currency, they have maintained stable funding by using a combination of medium- 
and long-term market funding and the acquisition of sticky corporate deposits. With 
customer channels becoming more digitalized and households' asset choices undergoing 
changes, banks need to continue to work toward establishing stable funding bases, while 
paying attention to changes in the funding environment.

Developments in corporate bankruptcies and defaults 
Corporate bankruptcies have been more or less unchanged, albeit with fluctuations (Chart IV-1-4). 
The upward trend in indicators of default rates since the pandemic has stabilized somewhat. The 
ratio of operating profits to sales for large manufacturing firms declined in the second quarter of 
2025, mainly due to the effects of the appreciation of the yen and the rise in tariffs, but remains at 
a high level. Corporate profits are on an improving trend overall (left panel of Chart IV-1-5). Under 
these circumstances, the proportion of financially vulnerable firms among small and medium-sized 
enterprises (SMEs), such as firms that are either making operating losses with negative net worth 
or are making operating losses, has been falling, likely contributing to the stabilization in the 
increase in corporate bankruptcies and defaults  (middle panel of Chart IV-1-5). However, the 
distribution of the ratio of operating profits to sales for SMEs, which widened during the pandemic, 
has not yet returned to pre-pandemic levels, and there are a considerable number of firms whose 
profit recovery has been more moderate than the overall trend (right panel of Chart IV-1-5). For 
these firms, in particular, rises in raw material prices, labor shortages, and rising labor costs may 
be adding further pressure.8 Furthermore, bankruptcies and defaults, which were held in check by 
the measures to support corporate financing implemented during the pandemic, may continue to 
occur with a delay, particularly among financially vulnerable firms.

i Objectives of the Financial System Report The Bank of Japan's Financial System Report has two main objectives. The first is to assess the stability of Japan's financial system. The second is to communicate with all related parties on the future tasks and challenges in order to ensure the system's stability. The Report assesses the vulnerabilities of the financial system from a macroprudential perspective. Within a macroprudential framework, institutional designs and policy measures are developed based on risk assessments in the financial system in order to ensure the stability of the overall financial system. In so doing, the interconnectedness of the real economy, financial markets, and financial institutions' behavior are taken into account. The Bank uses the results of the analysis set out in the Report in planning policies to ensure the stability of the financial system and for providing guidance and advice to financial institutions through on-site examinations and off-site monitoring. It makes use of the results in international discussions on regulation, supervision, and vulnerability assessment. In relation to the conduct of monetary policy, the macro assessment of financial system stability is also regarded as important input for the Bank in assessing risks in economic and price developments from a medium- to long- term perspective. Motivations behind the October 2025 issue At the beginning of April 2025, asset prices fluctuated significantly in global financial markets due to heightened uncertainties regarding trade policies in each jurisdiction. Currently, uncertainties remain high regarding the formulation of economic policies in each jurisdiction, and regarding geopolitical risks and developments in global financial markets. This Report analyzes the following four points. First, this Report analyzes the effects of changes in trade and other policies in each jurisdiction on domestic corporate sector and banks' credit costs. As a result of changes in trade and other policies

in each jurisdiction triggered by, for example, the materialization of geopolitical risks, global trade volume could fall substantially, adversely affecting corporate profits. This Report also provides an analysis of the resilience of the financial system if such tail risks were to materialize. Second, with regard to stock and real estate prices, the transaction environment in each market is examined, thereby providing an analysis of potential future risks. Third, this Report explores the possibility that foreign non-bank financial intermediaries (NBFIs), such as hedge funds, which have been increasing their presence both domestically and internationally, may have an effect on Japanese financial markets, particularly through the rapid unwinding of investment positions. Fourth, this Report provides updates on the effects of changes in the interest rate environment on banks, households, and firms. With regard to developments in deposits, this Report examines the effects of structural factors such as demographic changes and the spread of digital channels, and those of other factors that affect bank deposits amid rising interest rates.

Executive summary: Stability assessment of Japan's financial system Japan's financial system has been maintaining stability on the whole. In the loan market, financial intermediation has continued to function smoothly as firms' demand for loans has continued to rise and banks' lending stance has remained active. Under such circumstances, no major financial imbalances have been seen in current financial activities. Japanese banks have sufficient capital bases and stable funding bases to withstand significant stresses, including those equivalent to the global financial crisis that would cause major corrections in financial markets and the real economy at home and abroad, as well as those with compound factors particularly resulting from the materialization of geopolitical risks that would cause a substantial decline in global trade volume, and lead to global increases in inflation and interest rates. However, uncertainties remain high regarding the formulation of economic policies in each jurisdiction, and regarding geopolitical risks, and developments in global financial markets. Financial institutions need to be vigilant against the materialization of various risks. From a long- term perspective, if structural factors remain, such as a decline in firms' loan demand reflecting the shrinking population and other factors, banks' profitability and loss-absorbing capacity could decline, depending on the supply and demand balance in the loan market, and this could lead to a contraction of financial intermediation activities or an overheating, such as excessive search for yield. From the perspective of maintaining stability in Japan's financial system, close attention is warranted on future developments in the financial system, while examining both overheating and contraction risks (Chart I-1). Developments in asset prices  Chapters II, IV-B, and V-A In global financial markets, at the beginning of April, stock prices fell substantially as market sentiment became significantly cautious, reflecting

the heightened uncertainties regarding trade policy in each jurisdiction. Since then, prices of risky assets have risen, with market sentiment improving, reflecting factors such as progress in trade negotiations. The heat map shows that stock prices has been "red," which signals an upward deviation from the trend (Chart I-1). In terms of stock valuations as of the end of September, price-earnings (P/E) ratios remain generally at historical average levels while risk premiums indicated by the equity yield spreads, i.e., the difference between expected equity yields and 10-year Japanese government bond (JGB) yields, have declined somewhat (left panel of Chart I-2). Given that uncertainties regarding the formulation of trade and other economic policies in each jurisdiction remain high, sentiment in global financial markets could become cautious. Given that Japanese banks have a certain amount of market risk associated with stockholdings, close attention should be paid to developments in risky asset prices, including stock prices. Corporate bankruptcies and defaults and the effects of trade and other policies in each jurisdiction  Chapters IV-A and VI-B Amid the continuing moderate economic recovery, corporate profits in Japan have been improving on the whole, and the proportion of firms that are either making operating losses with negative net worth or are making operating losses, which increased during the pandemic, has been falling. Corporate bankruptcies and defaults have been more or less unchanged, albeit with fluctuations (Chart I-5). However, it is necessary to bear in mind that labor shortages, rising labor costs and rises in raw material prices may be adding further pressure. Although default probabilities also rise, the increase is small -- about 0.1 percentage points at the median -- reflecting firms' sound financial conditions, such as ample on-hand liquidity, prior to the stress event. However, given the large heterogeneity in firms' financial conditions, for those SMEs with strong downward pressure on their profits, there is a risk that default probabilities may rise as a result of diminishing on-hand liquidity and rising leverage to offset the decline in liquidity. Given the high degree of uncertainty surrounding the future direction of trade policies and their impact on the real economy, continued vigilance is warranted. Firms' resilience to rising interest rates Finally, firms' resilience to higher interest rates is examined. As summarized in the previous Report, the number of firms in the economy as a whole whose borrowings exceeding their cash and deposit holdings (firms whose interest-bearing debt exceeds their holdings of cash and deposits) is decreasing, and even among firms whose borrowings exceeding their cash and deposit holdings, the overall ICR has risen (Chart IV-1-12). Thus, credit management of loans to financially vulnerable firms continues to warrant attention. IV. Risks faced by financial institutions A. Credit risk 35 2. Foreign credit risk As of the end of fiscal 2024, Japanese banks' foreign credit risk has remained low (Chart IV-1-13). Non-performing loan (NPL) ratios and credit cost ratios have declined, affected by improvements among some large borrowers in the United States. Although loan-loss provision ratios have declined as a result of the aforementioned developments in large borrowers, loan-loss provision ratios have been at relatively high levels, partly due to forward-looking loan-loss provisioning, including for the effects of trade and other policies in each jurisdiction. The break-even credit cost ratio of banks' international business (net interest income on foreign loans/foreign loans outstanding) remains relatively high, and even if considerable credit costs were to be incurred, they could be absorbed by net interest income. The composition of foreign loans' credit ratings by type of product shows that the quality of banks' foreign loan portfolios has been maintained on the whole (Chart IV-1-14). Investment grade loans have continued to account for almost 70 percent of corporate loans overall. The rating composition of leveraged loans, which entail relatively high risk, has improved slightly due to a leveling-off in downgrades reflecting the effects of past interest rate increases. Turning to the rating composition of project finance loans, the share of investment grade loans has declined as banks have been selective in their lending based on profitability.
